corrections.why_faster: Standard-library algorithm, not language codegen. rust/src/benchmarks/sort_self.rs calls t.sort() on a cloned Vec<i32>; the rust-lang/rust source (library/alloc/src/slice.rs, 'Current implementation') states slice::sort is based on driftsort (Orson Peters, Lukas Bergdoll), a quicksort/mergesort hybrid with run detection; cpp/src/sort.cpp calls std::sort (libstdc++ introsort) on a copied vector, and the C version calls qsort with a comparator. Both sides copy the same unsorted 400,000-element array every iteration and the shared checksum (61757772 in run.js) guards the output, so the work is equal. Which driftsort component (branchless partitioning, small-sort networks) gives the 2.4x on random int32 was not isolated by the suite; that part is inference.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C++ 'prod' (make -j prod): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer -std=c++20; 'Fast': -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops with -flto=thin; 'Unsafe': -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer with -flto=full; PGO variants at -O2 (g++ 16.0.1 20260322 trunk, clang 22.1.8; no -stdlib flag, so both compilers use libstdc++ on Linux). corrections.caveats: Compares the stable Rust sort (driftsort) against C++ std::sort (unstable introsort), so the algorithms differ by design; the like-for-like C++ call would be std::stable_sort (not measured). The win belongs to Rust's standard library sort, not to the Rust language or compiler; the -O3 -march=native C++ builds (0.995-1.021 s) do not beat the -O2 prod G++ build (0.982 s). The Rust std sort work (ipnsort and driftsort) is also being catalogued from sort-research-rs by other wave-14 searches, so this row mostly adds an independent shootout measurement. Rust build is cargo release without LTO and is still faster than the C++ Fast/Unsafe/PGO builds. Workload is uniformly random int32 below 1,000,000 (n=400,000), 50 iterations, copy included in the timing on both sides. corrections.workload: LangArena Compress::BWTEncode: Burrows-Wheeler transform of 100,000 bytes made by repeating the 11-byte pattern 'ABRACADABRA' (generate_test_data), via cyclic prefix-doubling suffix sorting with a comparison sort over (rank[i], rank[(i+k)%n]) pairs; the doubling loop runs while k < n with no early exit, so 17 sort calls per transform; 30 iterations (run.js).
corrections.claimed_speedup: Rust 0.422 s vs C/Gcc/Fast 0.699 s (best of all C/C++ configurations), C/Gcc 0.725 s, C++/G++/Fast 1.056 s, C++/G++ 1.179 s, C++/Clang++ 1.259 s. About 1.7x faster than the best C/C++ configuration and 2.5x faster than the best C++ configuration (derived from page data). Rust/PGO 0.413 s, Rust/WASM/Node 0.386 s. Measured on a periodic input where, in the verifier's simulation of the same algorithm, 14 of the 17 sort calls receive an array that is already sorted.
corrections.why_faster: Standard-library sort adaptivity on presorted input, not language codegen. The Rust and C++ versions run the same prefix-doubling loop (Rust with usize ranks and 16-byte pairs, C++ with int32 pairs, so Rust moves more memory); Rust calls sa.sort_by (driftsort, documented in rust-lang/rust library/alloc/src/slice.rs as linear time on fully sorted input) and C++ calls std::sort (libstdc++ introsort, O(n log n) even on sorted input). A Python simulation of the same algorithm on the same 100,000-byte ABRACADABRA input (verifier, not the suite) found that, with a stable sort, the suffix array handed to the sort is a single ascending run in every round from k=8 to k=65536 (14 of 17 rounds); on random 5-letter input it is a single run from k=16 on, because ranks are all distinct and the loop never exits early. The C version uses two LSD counting-sort passes per round (a different, O(n) algorithm) and is still slower than Rust.
corrections.caveats: The win comes from the Rust standard-library stable sort (driftsort) detecting already-sorted input: in the verifier's simulation 14 of the 17 sort calls per transform receive a fully sorted suffix array on this periodic ABRACADABRA input, and any input becomes presorted once all ranks are distinct because the doubling loop has no early exit. It is therefore the same mechanism as the Sort::Self row, not an independent second reason, and the 1.7x does not carry over to a BWT/suffix-array implementation with an early exit or to a library such as libdivsufsort. Workload was mis-described as 'generated bytes'; it is a repeated 11-byte pattern. Rust uses 16-byte usize pairs against 8-byte int32 pairs in C++, so data layout does not explain the gap. Comparison sorts with indirect key lookups are cache-bound, so results may move with data size (100,000 bytes here). Rust/WASM/Node (0.386 s) beating native Rust suggests run-to-run noise of several percent. The Zig row (1.006 s) and Nim rows (0.854 s default) do not beat the best C row at default builds. Sources: cpp/src/compress.cpp, rust/src/benchmarks/compress.rs and c/src/compress.c in kostya/LangArena.
